title: The 1933 book, and Armstrong is the whole band
summary: The book mixed arrangements, heads and stocks; Armstrong told him not to be bothered by people saying he was the whole band, and they talked music and the Saints.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Tell me about that '33 band, on the road. Did you keep some -- well, you said that the other arranger had copied some of the things that you had arranged earlier, the '31 band.
So you had a pretty good book behind you this time, I guess, a library.
Yes, we did. We had a nice book, but it was a mixed book. Some arrangements, some heads, and some stock.

Did Louis really care too much how the band sounded? Did he ever say anything to you about, oh, the band sounds good tonight, or the saxes are out of tune or something like that? Because he was the star attraction.

Yeah, he was the star attraction. No, the only thing, he did say to me, he told me, he said, don't let -- people that was saying that about this first band, now, this was the first band. He told me, don't let this worry you, but the people say that Louis Armstrong is the whole band, and he told me, he said, don't pay any attention to that, don't let it worry you. Which, I guess he let me know not to feel dishearted or anything liked that. Because that's what people -- that's what a lot of them were saying, anyway. They were saying, Louis
Armstrong is the whole band. That meant that the band was nothing, but Louis Armstrong was the whole band, you see. But that didn't bother me.
Did you two ever -- I'm sure you must have -- just talked about music? What did you talk about?

Yes, we would talk about music and talk about arrangements and numbers that he would like for me to do, and one of them was, like I told you, When All the Saints Go Marching In, and Pops, that's in the bag.
